nameStory: The Milk-white Toothed Polypore gets its name from its creamy white color and its fascinating ability to produce different types of spore-bearing surfaces. Sometimes it forms tiny pores like other polypores, but under certain conditions it develops tooth-like projections that hang down like miniature icicles. This shape-shifting ability makes it one of the most adaptable crust fungi in our forests.
description: The Milk-white Toothed Polypore is a common crust fungus that forms thin, spreading patches on dead hardwood branches and logs. It appears as white to cream-colored crusts that can stretch several inches across the wood surface. Unlike mushrooms with caps and stems, this fungus grows flat against its host, sometimes developing a slightly shelf-like edge. The underside varies from having tiny pores to developing distinctive tooth-like projections, giving it its unique dual personality.

idTips.label: Surface Structure
idTips.description: The spore-bearing surface can show tiny pores or hanging tooth-like projections, sometimes both on the same specimen. Run your finger gently across it - the teeth feel like soft bristles while pores feel smooth with tiny holes.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Consistently white to cream-colored throughout, sometimes developing slight yellow or buff tones with age. Fresh specimens are bright white and feel slightly soft to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms spreading crusts that hug the wood surface tightly, often with thin, wavy edges that may curl slightly upward. The fungus can cover large areas of a single log.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels leathery but somewhat soft when fresh, becoming harder and more brittle as it dries. Has no particular smell or a faint musty wood odor.

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on dead hardwood branches, logs, and stumps. Rarely appears on conifers, preferring oak, maple, and other deciduous trees.

habitat: Throughout New England's forests, parks, and wooded areas on fallen hardwood logs and dead branches. Particularly common in mixed deciduous forests and urban areas with mature trees where fallen wood is left to decompose naturally. You'll often find it on the same log with other wood-decomposing fungi, creating colorful communities of different crust fungi species.

seasonality.spring: Fresh white growth begins appearing as moisture levels rise. Look for bright white, soft patches starting to spread across winter-weathered logs.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most vibrant specimens showing clear pore or tooth structures. The fungus actively spreads during humid periods following summer rains.
seasonality.fall: Mature specimens are easily spotted, often covering extensive areas of logs. Fall rains trigger new growth spurts before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Existing specimens become harder and more brittle but remain visible. Growth slows significantly, but established colonies persist through freezing weather.

funFact: This shape-shifting fungus is so adaptable that scientists have accidentally described it as dozens of 'new' species over the years, not realizing they were all looking at the same remarkably variable organism - it's like the fungal equivalent of a master of disguise!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other white crust fungi, but the variable surface structure (pores AND teeth) is distinctive. If you see what looks like two different white fungi growing together - one with pores and one with teeth - it's probably just one very confused Milk-white Toothed Polypore showing off its dual personality.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'polypore' (meaning 'many pores'), this fungus doesn't always have pores - a perfect example of how common names in mycology can be misleading. The scientific community has been fooled by its variability so many times that it holds the record for one of the longest lists of synonyms (different scientific names) for a single species.
compareHints: Its closest relative in New England, the Frothy Porecrust, lacks the distinctive tooth-like projections and maintains a more consistently porous surface. The Milk-white Toothed Polypore's ability to switch between pores and teeth makes it unique among local crust fungi. When in doubt, look for the telltale teeth - no other common white crust fungus in our region develops these hanging projections.
